# Per-package minimum fuzz-target count: a ratchet, so discovery failing is
# never mistaken for a clean campaign.
#
# There are two distinct ways for discovery to break, and run-fuzz.sh checks
# both, because the first check is blind to the second:
#
#   1. targets renamed away from Fuzz*, package still in the list
#      -> the package lists FEWER targets than its number here, and the
#         per-package ratchet inside the fuzzing loop fails the run.
#
#   2. the package dropped from the list entirely (an upstream sync editing
#      DEFAULT_PACKAGES in fuzz.yml, say)
#      -> the loop never reaches it, so the ratchet above says nothing: every
#         remaining package meets its minimum and the run goes green with all of
#         that package's targets unfuzzed. --require-complete catches this by
#         asserting, after the loop, that every package with a non-zero minimum
#         here was in the list. The weekly run over DEFAULT_PACKAGES passes the
#         flag; a workflow_dispatch naming a subset deliberately does not.
#
# The global "no targets at all" check cannot do either job: two targets are
# inherited from go-ethereum and are not going anywhere
# (core/vm FuzzPrecompiledContracts, core/vm/runtime FuzzVmRuntime), so the
# total is >= 2 unconditionally under both failure modes.
#
# Counts may only go UP. After landing new targets, refresh with:
#
#   .github/scripts/fuzz/run-fuzz.sh --write-baseline ./pkg...
#
# and commit the result in the same PR. A package listing MORE targets than
# recorded is a notice asking for that refresh, not a failure, so a fuzz PR is
# never blocked on it. Removing a package from fuzz.yml on purpose means dropping
# its line here in the same PR — that is what makes check 2 above a decision
# rather than an accident.
#
# <package> <minimum targets>
./config 1
./consensus/misc/eip1559 1
./consensus/misc/eip4844 1
./consensus/parlia 16
./core/vm 3
./core/vm/runtime 3
./core/vm/systemcontract 2
./params 2
